summary:
WHAT I DID. I read src/spine/{lever,assemble,units,wire,gate,compose,derive,registry,rng}.py, extracted the module docstring of every src/*/api.py and src/*/levers.py by AST, parsed ASSEMBLY_ORDER and LOOP_ORDER as data, ran spine.assemble.build(), ran spine.compose.compose(), ran all seven test files in tests/, and cross-checked every number against .rework/ISSUES.md PART 2 and notes/05_ERRORS.md's invalidation list. Everything below is from a file I read or a command I ran.

WHAT THE SYSTEM IS TODAY. It is a DECLARED, MOSTLY-UNIMPLEMENTED SYSTEM. There are 13 packages under src/ plus a non-package spine/. Every package has exactly three files that matter: __init__.py (a marker with no code, deliberately), levers.py (the package's configuration declarations), and api.py (its frozen public signature set). 262 levers are declared across the 13 levers.py files. 131 public entry points are declared across the 13 api.py files, and 94 of them are stubs whose body is `raise NotImplementedError`; 37 have real bodies. compose(environ={}) executes and stops at the first stub, which today is CAP.startup_refusals — it gets through RUN's process setup, the resume read, RUN/WORLD refusals, LM geometry, the corpus open, vocabulary build, the geometry gate, the data plan, epoch-0 draw, tokenize, model build, signature, fabric, world, store, partition and the valve constructor before it stops. So the skeleton runs; the mechanisms mostly do not exist yet. There is no training loop in src/ at all — compose.py says so explicitly ("IT DOES NOT RUN A TRAINING LOOP") and LOOP_ORDER is a reading order for whoever writes one.

THE OWNERSHIP SPINE. The problem it solves is stated in numbers the repo counts for itself: the old tree kept 328 knobs in one `_SPEC` table with hand-typed owner comments that drifted (LOSS_MASK_DEAD tagged `# tokenizer` inside the `--- domains ---` block; 41 knobs filed under `misc`), values were materialised as module globals and read anywhere via `_env`/`_i`/`_f` with each call site restating its own default, and modules read os.environ directly behind the registry's back. The spine's answer: a lever is a class attribute on exactly ONE LeverSet subclass and its environment name is GENERATED as f"{PREFIX}_{FIELD.upper()}", so there is no `name=` parameter and no owner comment to drift; the default must be a literal, checked at declaration; `LeverSet.from_env()` is the only code permitted to name os.environ; and a resolved Config is frozen. What it GUARANTEES is narrower than the marketing, and the code says so at length: a module cannot MINT a foreign Config (O1 no os.environ, O3 no two lever sets, O8 no from_env outside spine/assemble.py), a function cannot hold two Configs by signature (O9), and a runtime latch closes from_env after build() returns. What it does NOT stop is a caller HANDING a foreign Config to a function — `memory_prune(configs["FAB"])` returning FAB_SLOTS was reproduced by a reviewer. `Config.owned_by("MEM")` is the assertion at the read site, and O9 requires it of annotated parameters; unannotated parameters remain uncovered. IMPORTANT FOR A README: .rework/PLAN.md:57 still carries the retracted overclaim ("reading a foreign lever is a NameError at author time"), which lever.py:32 and assemble.py:9-11 both explicitly correct as false. Do not repeat it.

LEVER / WIRE / COUPLING. A LEVER is one declared knob owned by one package, carrying default + help + unit + optional choices; read as `cfg.field`. A COUPLING is a row in `spine/assemble.py::COUPLINGS` — a value computed from more than one lever, with declared sources, a destination `PREFIX.d_field`, a `compute` function and a mandatory prose reason. A WIRE is a coupling whose sources cross a package boundary; it goes in the `Wires` ledger, spends budget, and widens `affects()`. A coupling whose sources are all in the destination's own package is LOCAL — still `d_`-prefixed, but not a wire and not budgeted. Live counts from build(): 23 coupling rows = 19 cross-package wires (budget 25) + 4 local. The destination name is chosen by the WIRE, not the receiver, and `Config._wire` refuses any name not starting with `d_` — so `grep -rn 'd_' src/` enumerates every coupling. `affects(L)` is computed from the ledger rather than hand-written, because a hand-maintained table would be authored by the same person whose leak the isolation sweep exists to catch.

CLOCK KINDS. units.py declares six: Steps, Flushes, Windows, Backwards, Epochs, Selections. They are NOT int subclasses — deliberately, since `class Steps(int)` would let `Steps(4000) >= 250` pass silently. Comparison, arithmetic and even `==` across kinds raise UnitError; the only legal crossing is `convert(to, per)` with an explicit rate. They exist because 32 of the survey's 475 defect records are unit mismatches and the recurring one is a clock: pin_tick counted FLUSHES against a threshold declared in STEPS (16x slow at BATCH_W=16), the capacity valve's clock counted calls not steps, and four subsystems' modulo cadences never coincided with a flush step so they never fired. Non-clock units (BYTES, TOKENS, BITS_PER_BYTE, FRACTION, ...) are metadata only, never enforced.

DID IT FIRE. gate.py holds one frozen dataclass, `Gate(name, fired, value, threshold, reachable, reason)`, with THREE states that must never collapse: FIRED; armed-and-did-not-fire (a real measurement); and UNREACHABLE (the condition cannot be met on this configuration — not a measurement at all, and a `reason` is REQUIRED on that arm, enforced in __post_init__). The counts behind it: 57 of 475 records are mechanisms armed and inert while the report said nothing, and 60 more are guards whose condition could not be satisfied. Gate.line() always prints the arithmetic (`value vs threshold`), including on the unreachable arm. `NotBuilt` is a separate exception, deliberately NOT subclassing NotImplementedError, because NotImplementedError is a MARKER in this tree for "P4 has not written this yet" and the tooling counts it. Every one of the 134 entry-point docstrings in src/*/api.py carries a `DID IT FIRE:` block naming the counters that would prove the mechanism ran.

THE COMPOSITION ROOT. src/spine/compose.py. It holds every package's Config and every package's objects at once, because O10 forbids one package importing another, so a cross-package value must arrive as an argument the spine passed in. It exposes `plan()` (returns the two order tables as data, calling nothing) and `compose(environ, restored=None)` (resolves all 13 Configs via spine.assemble.build, then builds objects in order). ASSEMBLY_ORDER has 39 rows across stages process/resume/refuse/geometry/corpus/restore/vocab/gate/plan/stream/segment/model/signature/fabric/world/store/partition/valve/optimizer/clock/epoch0/warmup/cadence/audit/persist/retention/signal. LOOP_ORDER has 58 rows across five stages driven by one RunClock: E (per epoch), A (per window), B (per flush), C (the checkpoint fan-out, an event not a clock), R (the report, once). Every row is a 4- or 5-tuple whose fifth element names what the row PRODUCES, spelled as the CONSUMING signature spells it — that column exists so "nothing supplies this argument" is decidable. 23 entry points are declared in DEFERRED_ENTRY_POINTS with the missing producer as the reason; 24 entries in ROW_ARGUMENTS_ELSEWHERE.

THE AMBITION SENTENCE — the parent's guess needs correcting. The canonical statement is notes/00_INDEX.md:24-36: "A byte-level language model with five things bolted to it, each of which can be turned off: 1. a dynamic BPE tokenizer that mints new merges during training; 2. the Fabric — a preallocated population of low-rank expert adapters, routed per window, born, ranked, mutated and culled during the run; 3. a self-organising domain assembler that clusters the stream into domains from a learned signature space, with no labels; 4. an editable external memory — a surprise-gated kNN store of context→token pairs that can be read, re-keyed, flagged wrong, and deleted per entry or per source; 5. a world model that predicts the next latent state." FIVE, not four, and the domain assembler and the signature space it clusters in are two separate packages (DOM and SIG) in the rebuild. The phrase "society of independent experts" is the OLD README's and is misleading — it is the Fabric's `society` forward arm, not an ExpertBank/ExpertRouter population (that mechanism is dropped by the census). Do not use it.

WHAT IS FOR THE README AUTHOR TO AVOID. The current README.md:83-136 is the old-tree landing page. Its headline "-0.0009 collateral" is retracted three ways (notes/08_GLOSSARY.md:230 calls it "not reproducible at HEAD and not the project's stated goal"; INV-13 voids every arm comparison before 2026-08-13; .rework/ISSUES.md P2-C3 catalogues it). It also directs readers to STATE.md, garry/GARRY.md and CL_TESTBED.md, none of which exist at those paths any more (all moved under archive/). Two prose-vs-tree drifts are LIVE and failing in the test suite right now: tests/test_assemble.py:173 says 261 levers where the tree has 262, and docs/04_CONTRACT.md:218 says DATA has 17 levers where it has 18. Also note the task's premise is partly wrong: self_organize.py, memory.py, tokenizer.py, vocab.py, datastream.py and world_model.py are all still at the REPOSITORY ROOT, not under archive/. archive/ holds garry/, legacy/, handoff/, docs/, STATE.md, CL_TESTBED.md and agent-transcripts/.

claims.claim: src/ contains exactly 13 lever-owning packages plus a non-package 'spine' directory. The 13 directory names are capacity, ckpt, data, domains, eval, fabric, lm, memory, opt, sig, tok, train, world; their PREFIXes are CAP, CKPT, DATA, DOM, EVAL, FAB, LM, MEM, OPT, SIG, TOK, RUN, WORLD.
claims.source: ls src/; python3 -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'src');from spine.assemble import PACKAGES;print(sorted(PACKAGES))" -> ['CAP','CKPT','DATA','DOM','EVAL','FAB','LM','MEM','OPT','RUN','SIG','TOK','WORLD']; src/spine/compose.py::APIS
claims.caveat: Two PREFIXes do not match their directory: src/train/ owns PREFIX 'RUN' and src/capacity/ owns 'CAP'. src/train/__init__.py states this is deliberate: 'THE DIRECTORY IS `train` AND THE PREFIX IS `RUN`, deliberately and not by oversight ... the environment name is generated from the PREFIX, never from the directory'.

claims.claim: Each package owns exactly one line of purpose, taken verbatim from the first line of its levers.py docstring: CAP 'the earned-capacity valve: the one mechanism that lets a run become bigger than it was'; CKPT 'the run's persistent state: where it is written, where a run continues from, and what is kept'; DATA 'the bytes the run trains on: which corpora, in what order, cut where, and what is held back'; DOM 'the self-assembling partition: where the stream is cut, what the pieces are called, and which of those names are allowed to survive'; EVAL 'the instruments: how much is measured, how long, how often, and where the verdict line sits'; FAB 'the expert population: who exists, who gets the token, who is born, who is removed'; LM 'the base language model: which network is built, how big it is, and what a new symbol costs it'; MEM 'the editable store: what gets written into it, what gets thrown out of it, and how it is read'; OPT 'the schedule and the optimiser: the one absolute learning rate, its shape over time, and the size of the batch that rate is applied to'; SIG 'the signature encoder: the one description of a window that every router reads'; TOK 'the online byte-BPE: what the run's symbols ARE, and when they are allowed to change'; RUN 'the training loop: how long the run is, what root of randomness it starts from, what machine it runs on, how that machine's arithmetic is executed, and which half of the program runs at all'; WORLD 'the world model: a latent state for the observed stream, and a population that predicts it forward'.

The loop is RUN package mechanism -- RunClock.advance is the only site in the tree that increments a counter, and Cadences.due is the only cadence primitive. claims.claim: ASSEMBLY_ORDER has 39 rows and LOOP_ORDER has 58 rows, both declared as tuples of tuples and returned as data by spine.compose.plan() without calling anything.

claims.claim: LOOP_ORDER has five stages, all driven by one RunClock: E = per EPOCH (runs before the first window of an epoch and again on Tick.rolled); A = per WINDOW, above the batch accumulator; B = per FLUSH; C = the CHECKPOINT FAN-OUT, an EVENT not a clock, entered from three routes; R = the REPORT, once, after Tick.finished.
claims.source: src/spine/compose.py, comment block immediately above LOOP_ORDER: 'FIVE STAGES, all driven by the one RunClock: E = per EPOCH ... A = per WINDOW, above the batch accumulator. B = per FLUSH. C = the CHECKPOINT FAN-OUT. An EVENT, not a clock ... R = the REPORT, once, after Tick.finished.'
claims.caveat: The same comment records a consequence worth stating: RUN.epochs defaults to 1, advance() sets both `rolled` and `finished` on the single roll a default run takes, and `finished` WINS -- so 'THE E ROWS IN THIS TABLE NEVER RUN ON A ONE-EPOCH RUN'. Epoch 0's material comes from ASSEMBLY_ORDER instead.

claims.claim: Every ASSEMBLY_ORDER/LOOP_ORDER row is a 4- or 5-tuple; the fifth element names what that row PRODUCES for later rows, spelled the way the CONSUMING signature spells it, and a row that produces nothing a later row consumes keeps four elements deliberately.
claims.source: src/spine/compose.py comment above ASSEMBLY_ORDER: 'Every row is (stage, PREFIX, entry point, what it receives that is not its own Config, what it PRODUCES for later rows). A row that yields nothing a later row consumes ... keeps FOUR elements, and that is a statement rather than a default.' Verified by parsing: rows have len 4 or 5.
claims.caveat: The same comment records why the fifth column was added: two mechanical heuristics were tried and both failed (30 findings and 25 findings respectively), because the tables could not separate PRODUCED BY AN EARLIER ROW from MENTIONED IN PASSING until they recorded what a row produces.

claims.claim: 23 entry points are declared in DEFERRED_ENTRY_POINTS — the list of entry points the order tables do not yet reach, each with the phase that will reach it and the argument that has no producer. They are: CAP.observe, CKPT.Retention.consider, EVAL.coherence, EVAL.curve_probe, EVAL.generate, EVAL.holdout_probe, EVAL.null_excess, EVAL.verdicts, EVAL.verification_fit, EVAL.wrongness_probe, FAB.Population.n, FAB.contribution, MEM.blend, MEM.judge, MEM.read, RUN.Timing.span, RUN.Timing.spans, TOK.Vocabulary.at_cap, TOK.Vocabulary.blen, TOK.Vocabulary.decode, TOK.Vocabulary.live_size, TOK.Vocabulary.size, WORLD.manage.

claims.caveat: compose.py's docstring states this table 'is checked backwards -- an entry a row now names is reported stale -- so it cannot become the place orphans go to be forgotten'. Note the whole retrieval read path (MEM.read/blend/judge) and almost all of EVAL are in here.

claims.claim: The ownership spine replaces a table of 328 knobs whose owner was a hand-typed comment. Two named symptoms of the drift: LOSS_MASK_DEAD is tagged '# tokenizer' inside the '--- domains ---' block, and 41 knobs are filed under 'misc'.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py module docstring, 'THE FAILURE THIS REPLACES'; the misc figure is corroborated by .rework/CENSUS.md 'The old tree filed 40 knobs under misc and 16 under report -- neither is an owner'
claims.caveat: lever.py says 41 under misc and CENSUS.md says 40 under misc plus 16 under report, with the .rework/CENSUS.md 'misc (41)' section heading listing 41. The one-off is unreconciled in the sources; if you cite it, say 'about 40'.

claims.claim: Ownership is the namespace, not a tag: a lever is a class attribute on exactly one LeverSet subclass and its environment name is GENERATED as f"{PREFIX}_{FIELD.upper()}". There is no name= parameter, so a name cannot be attached to a foreign owner.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py, 'OWNERSHIP IS THE NAMESPACE, NOT A TAG' paragraph and Lever.env_name_for(prefix)
claims.caveat: The prefix is deliberately never cached on the Lever object. lever.py::Lever.__set_name__ records why: an earlier version wrote v.prefix = cls.PREFIX onto the Lever, so a Lever reachable from two classes took whichever prefix was defined last, silently retargeting a base class's lever to a subclass's env name with every static check still passing.

claims.claim: A lever's default must be a literal, checked at declaration time in Lever.__init__ rather than by an AST rule.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py::Lever.__init__: 'if not isinstance(default, (int, float, str, bool, type(None))): raise LeverError("default must be a literal ... A value derived from another lever is a WIRE, not a default")'
claims.caveat: The stated reason is a specific old-tree failure: nine knobs whose default was another knob, e.g. MAX_DOMAINS = _i("MAX_DOMAINS", _i("FAB_NMAX", 4096)), which reads FAB_NMAX eagerly and poisons the 'nothing read this knob' audit.

claims.claim: LeverSet.from_env() is the only code in the tree permitted to name os.environ, and this is checked mechanically.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py::LeverSet.from_env docstring; tests/test_ownership.py check O1 'os.environ is named in exactly one file' -> PASS
claims.caveat: lever.py records that the old tree needed this: 'tokenizer.py read TOK_MINT_PMIN and TOK_MINT_GATE_K straight from os.environ, invisible to the registry and to every audit built on it'.

claims.claim: A resolved Config is immutable and frozen. _freeze() replaces the value mappings with types.MappingProxyType, not merely setting a flag.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py::Config._freeze
claims.caveat: The code records that the first version set a _frozen flag which only _wire consulted, so `cfg._vals['slots'] = 8` walked straight past the refusal — 'reproduced'. Worth stating as an example of the repo's method: the guarantee is written next to the defect that forced it.

claims.claim: The ownership spine's guarantee is NARROWER than 'a package cannot read another package's levers'. What is structural: a module may not name os.environ (O1), may not hold two lever sets under any spelling (O3), and may not call from_env outside spine/assemble.py (O8) — so a module cannot MINT a foreign Config. Being HANDED one is not prevented.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py module docstring, 'WHAT OWNERSHIP DOES NOT BUY' paragraph; and src/spine/assemble.py module docstring, 'WHAT THAT BUYS, STATED CORRECTLY THIS TIME'
claims.caveat: Both files record the same reproduced counterexample verbatim: `def memory_prune(cfg): return cfg.slots` called as `memory_prune(configs["FAB"])` returns 2048 with no error. Both files state that an earlier version of their own docstring called this 'an author-time NameError' and that this was false.

claims.claim: .rework/PLAN.md:57 still carries the retracted overclaim: 'A package receives only its own record as a parameter, so `def cull(pop, fab: FabricLevers, ...)` has no `mem`, `tok` or `dom` in scope: reading a foreign lever is a NameError at author time, not a policy.'
claims.source: grep -n NameError .rework/PLAN.md -> line 57; contradicted by src/spine/lever.py:32 'which a reviewer ran, against docstrings in this file and in spine/assemble.py that called it an "author-time NameError". It is not one.'
claims.caveat: This is the single most important thing for a README author not to copy. PLAN.md is a proposal document whose own header says 'Status: proposed, not started. Nothing in src/ exists yet' — it predates the correction.

claims.claim: Config.owned_by(prefix) is the only owner check that happens at the point of use. It raises naming both packages, returns self so it composes, and tests/test_ownership.py's O9 requires the call of any function outside the spine that annotates a parameter as a Config, with the prefix as a string literal.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py::Config.owned_by docstring and body; tests/test_ownership.py O9 'no function outside the wiring file receives two packages' Configs' -> PASS
claims.caveat: owned_by's own docstring says what it cannot see: 'a function that takes an UNANNOTATED parameter and never asserts. O9 cannot require an assertion it has no way to know is needed'. It is an assertion, not a capability: a function that never calls it is exactly as exposed as before.

claims.claim: There is a process-wide assembly latch: build() calls from_env exactly 13 times and then sets a module flag, after which any from_env call raises. This closes the runtime half of routes that no name-based check can see.
claims.source: src/spine/lever.py::_close_assembly/_reopen_assembly/assembly_closed and the refusal at the head of from_env
claims.caveat: lever.py is explicit about the latch's limits and about not overselling it: it is 'Not a security boundary and not described as one'; it does NOT close the DECLARATION half — `sib._levers["alpha"].default` reads a foreign lever with no from_env call and no Config, and only the behavioural L3 sweep could catch that. That sweep, tests/test_lever_isolation.py, DOES NOT EXIST (verified: ls returns 'No such file or directory').

claims.claim: A WIRE is a recorded coupling that crosses a package boundary. The destination field name is part of the wire record and the wire performs the assignment itself via Wires.add(..., into=cfg) -> Config._wire, so the receiving package never chooses the name it arrives under; Config._wire refuses any name not starting with 'd_'.
claims.source: src/spine/wire.py module docstring and Wires.add; src/spine/lever.py::Config._wire
claims.caveat: The stated consequence is checkable and worth quoting: 'a plain `grep -rn "d_" src/` enumerates every coupling in the system, with no tooling, no AST pass and nothing to keep in sync.' This answers a design-review objection quoted verbatim in both files: 'wires launder couplings -- fab.nmax arrives in domains as expert_slots and looks owned'.

claims.claim: The live coupling ledger holds 23 coupling rows: 19 cross-package wires against a WIRE_BUDGET of 25, plus 4 intra-package (local) derivations. NOT_WIRES holds 7 rejected candidates.
claims.source: python3 build(environ={}) -> len(wires)=19, budget=25, len(COUPLINGS)=23, len(NOT_WIRES)=7; tests/test_contract.py LIVE COUNTS 'couplings=23, intra_couplings=4, not_wires=7, wire_budget=25, wires=19'
claims.caveat: docs/04_CONTRACT.md:52-56 states these same four numbers and explicitly warns 'Do not restate these numbers elsewhere ... any prose copy is one that can go stale in silence -- this one had.' Take that warning literally for a README.

claims.claim: The 19 live wires and the packages they connect: FAB.slots -> DOM.d_expert_slots, MEM.d_owner_blocks, MEM.d_capacity, MEM.d_source_slots, CAP.d_expert_slots; OPT.batch_windows -> FAB.d_manage_period; OPT.batch_windows + CAP.pin_windows -> FAB.d_cap_lift_period and TOK.d_cap_lift_period; LM.vocab_slots -> TOK.d_vocab_ceiling and CAP.d_vocab_slots; CKPT.dir -> TOK.d_vocab_save_path; CKPT.resume -> TOK.d_vocab_read_path; TOK.max_bytes -> LM.d_max_token_bytes; LM.mask_dead_rows -> CAP.d_mask_dead_rows; FAB.pressure + FAB.slots -> CAP.d_operating_population; FAB.comp_ema -> DOM.d_comp_ema; FAB.comp_protect -> DOM.d_comp_protect; OPT.lr -> FAB.d_base_lr; OPT.lr_min_frac -> FAB.d_lr_min_frac. The 4 local derivations are FAB.d_operating_population, LM.d_pos_max, OPT.d_effective_batch_windows, SIG.d_idle_cadence.
claims.source: python3 build(environ={}) then iterating wires and diffing wires.dsts() against every Config's wired() keys
claims.caveat: Values shown are at the empty environment (all defaults). EVAL, DATA, RUN, WORLD and CKPT receive no wires at all; EVAL and RUN and DATA and WORLD emit none either.

claims.claim: affects(L) = {owner(L)} union {owner(d) : L in reads(d)} and is COMPUTED from the ledger, never declared in a table.
claims.source: src/spine/wire.py::Wires.affects and the module docstring section 'WHY affects() IS COMPUTED HERE AND NOT WRITTEN DOWN (graft G1)'
claims.caveat: The stated reason is worth repeating because it generalises: 'A hand-maintained AFFECTS = {...} table would be written by the same person whose leak the sweep exists to catch: they add the lever, they add its reach, and the sweep is permanently green for that lever from the day it is declared.' affects() is deliberately ONE HOP, and Wire.__init__ refuses a wire whose source is itself a d_ field to keep it so.

claims.claim: units.py declares exactly six clock kinds: Steps (optimizer steps), Flushes (batch flushes), Windows (stream windows, what `step` counts), Backwards (backward passes), Epochs (passes over the stream), Selections (times an expert was chosen).

claims.claim: Clock is deliberately NOT an int subclass, and cross-kind comparison, addition, subtraction AND equality all raise UnitError. The only legal crossing is convert(to, per) with an explicit positive rate.
claims.source: src/spine/units.py::Clock — '_same' raises on type mismatch for +, -, ==, <, <=, >, >=; convert() is the documented sole path
claims.caveat: units.py records that __eq__ raising was a correction: the first version returned plain False across kinds, so `Flushes(10) == Steps(10)` was quietly False and `Steps(4000) == 4000` was quietly False — 'a mismatch reported as a legitimate answer, in the module whose entire mechanism is that a cross-kind comparison cannot pass silently'.

claims.claim: The clock types exist because of specific measured defects, named in units.py: pin_tick counted FLUSHES against a threshold declared in STEPS (16x slow at BATCH_W=16); the capacity valve's clock counted calls, not steps; four subsystems' modulo cadences never coincided with a flush step so they never fired; and `step` advances per WINDOW while the loop body runs per FLUSH.
claims.source: src/spine/units.py module docstring, numbered point 2
claims.caveat: units.py is explicit that unit typing is narrow ON PURPOSE: only clocks are runtime-typed. Every other unit (bytes, bits/byte, fractions) is metadata, printed but never enforced, because 'static unit inference over arbitrary Python arithmetic is a type-inference engine with no type system underneath it'.

claims.claim: The DID IT FIRE discipline is one frozen dataclass, spine/gate.py::Gate(name, fired, value, threshold, reachable, reason), with three states that must not collapse: FIRED; fired=False + reachable=True (armed and did not fire — a measurement); and reachable=False (the condition CANNOT be met on this configuration — not a measurement at all). A reason is REQUIRED on the unreachable arm, enforced in __post_init__.
claims.source: src/spine/gate.py::Gate and Gate.__post_init__ ('Gate {name!r} is declared unreachable with no reason. UNREACHABLE without a reason is indistinguishable from armed-and-inert to every reader of the report')
claims.caveat: Gate.line() always prints the arithmetic '(value vs threshold)' including on the unreachable arm; gate.py records that the first version dropped the numbers there, which is 'the same verdict without the arithmetic this record exists to refuse'.

claims.claim: Gate lives in the spine rather than in each package because all 13 packages must print the same three states in the same shape. It reads no lever, holds no state and imports nothing.
claims.source: src/spine/gate.py module docstring: 'Thirteen private Gate classes would be thirteen chances for one of them to collapse the last two states'
claims.caveat: gate.py cites 57 armed-but-inert and 60 untrippable-guard records as the two bugs the two states distinguish: 'Those are two different bugs and they need two different words.'

claims.claim: gate.py also declares NotBuilt, an exception for a mechanism that is DECLARED and deliberately NOT BUILT. It deliberately does not subclass NotImplementedError.
claims.source: src/spine/gate.py::NotBuilt docstring
claims.caveat: The reason is mechanical, not stylistic: in this tree `raise NotImplementedError` is a MARKER that tests/test_contract.py::k13_live_counts and tools/sync_counts.py both count textually. Overloading it made FAB.build (which has a full body) count as a stub, so the documented progress numbers said one more entry point was unwritten than actually was.

claims.claim: The canonical statement of what the system is, as five components on a byte-level LM, is notes/00_INDEX.md:24-36: (1) a dynamic BPE tokenizer that mints new merges DURING training so vocabulary and segmentation both move while the model learns against them; (2) the Fabric — a preallocated population of low-rank expert adapters, routed per window, born, ranked, mutated and culled during the run; (3) a self-organising domain assembler that clusters the stream into domains from a learned signature space, with no labels; (4) an editable external memory — a surprise-gated kNN store of context->token pairs that can be read, re-keyed, flagged wrong, and deleted per entry or per source; (5) a world model that predicts the next latent state. Each can be turned off.
claims.source: notes/00_INDEX.md, section 'What the system is'
claims.caveat: It is FIVE, not four. The rebuild splits component 3 into two packages: DOM (the partition) and SIG (the signature space it clusters in). The list maps onto packages as TOK, FAB, DOM+SIG, MEM, WORLD — with LM the byte-level model itself and DATA, OPT, CAP, CKPT, RUN, EVAL the supporting spine. notes/00_INDEX.md describes the OLD tree, but every one of the five survives as a named package in src/.
